Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If you had a love marriage and your native languages are different, in which language are your children proficient? Mother's? Father's? Both? Neither, but in English or some other language?
Answer: I’m one such child. My parents had a love marriage. My father is a Tamil; and mom, a Kannadiga. Both of them were born and brought up in the South Indian Union Territory of Pondicherry. My father’s family was originally from the Delta region of Tamil Nadu (Thanjavur and surrounding districts). My mother’s family migrated to Tamil Nadu at least two centuries back and thereafter to Pondicherry in the late 1960’s. Consequently, my mother was raised speaking Kannada at home, and Tamil (official language of Pondicherry) outside home: in school and college. At home, we mostly speak Tamil since we live in a Tamil speaking region and most contacts outside home are Tamils. Also, my dad isn’t very fluent in Kannada; he does comprehend what’s spoken and attempts speaking short futile sentences, warranting bursts of laughter from mom and me. On the other hand, my maternal relatives speak only Kannada in their homes. Many many years after their migration to Tamil Nadu, they still follow the religious customs and tradition of Karnataka. Interaction between mom and them have till date been in no language but Kannada. Given this scenario, I had a strong exposure to both the languages. As a child, I often visited my relatives and grew up listening to a lot of Kannada. When my mom also joined, we all spoke in Kannada. Back home, I learnt English, French (Pondicherry, you know!) and Tamil. I developed a strong liking for the Tamil language and literature, thanks to my school teachers! In the last two to three years, I learnt to read and write (since I was already fluent in speaking) Kannada. Moreover, I have many friends and professional contacts from Bengaluru and other parts of Karnataka. So, I’m officially bilingual now, fluent in the native languages of both mom and dad! Me, with mom and dad <3

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Have you ever lost any respect for someone instantly?
Answer: Yes! This question reflexly reminds me of a scene at the coffee-counter of a Bengaluru restaurant. It might have easily been a year ago! Well, I was at this restaurant opposite to our hospital at Rajajinagar, waiting for my cup of coffee. I’d been in the locality for a while and the person handling the coffee counter is a quiet, unassuming and pleasant guy, as I know him. As I was waiting, I couldn’t help but hear the conversation the lady customer before me in the queue was having with the coffee guy. The conversation was in Kannada. I have included the English translation within parentheses. Lady: Enuuu, ninne kaaNle illa…! elli hogidri? (Where had you gone yesterday? you were not seen around!) Coffee guy: Huun, ninne bandirlilla. Maganige laptop kodsbekithu. (Yes, I had not come yesterday. I had to buy my son a laptop.) Lady: First hand a, second hand a?! (A new one or second-hand one?!) Coffee guy (quite abashed): First hand e ne (A new one indeed) That moment, my respect for that lady came crashing down! I’d never lost respect for a stranger that quickly ever before. Whilst it might be deemed a very normal conversation by many, personally I would never ever ask such a weird question! I might ask for the price, make, or if it was touchscreen, but never if it was second-hand! I kept wondering what kind of thought process a person should possess to make him/ her think that the child of a restaurant worker should get only ‘second-hand’ things in life! The fact that, that was the first question which popped in her mind only makes it worse. Just not done!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What are your views on Dr. Thamizhisai resigning her governor post?
Answer: It came in as a surprise! Believe me or not, I had googled ‘Can Indian Governors/ Presidents go back to electoral politics?’ just two days prior to her resignation! After losing the Tuticorin Lok Sabha Constituency to Kanimozhi in 2019, Dr. Tamilisai apparently quit electoral politics. Shortly, she was made the Governor of Telangana and a couple of years later, given the additional charge of Lieutenant Governor (LG) of Pondicherry. As a native Pondicherrian, I had never seen an LG who was as active as Dr. Tamilisai. Despite criticisms of her being a BJP stooge, she kept discharging her constitutional duties effectively. She broke the invisible barrier between the general public and the LG office! Being a Tamilian helped her connect with the public much better than the previous LGs, who were almost always from the North/ North-East. Within days of her assuming the LG post in February 2021, the then Congress Government collapsed leading to the imposition of LG rule until May 2021. This was also the period when COVID-19 second wave was peaking! I still remember her visit to the COVID-ICU and COVID casualty of the Medical College I graduated from. Being a doctor herself, she acknowledged the difficulties and challenges faced by the healthcare professionals, which is otherwise least expected from politicians! Probably, being the constitutional head was a hindrance for her to voice out her opinions and serve the people directly! That’s what she had told in her press interview following resignation as well. However, Dr. Tamilisai has the infamous record of having lost every election she had contested in previously (both MP and MLA elections)! I wish luck favours her this time. I am curious to know how she would function as a people’s representative, having seen her closely in a nominated role! Will her stint as Governor/ LG help her garner more votes this time? Will her contesting from Chennai South have an impact on her vote share?! We have to wait and watch! (Image Source: Google Images)

Question: What were your 12th marks, and what are you doing now?
Answer: Here is my 12th (popularly called Higher Secondary Course) marksheet! Despite a BPC (Biology-Physics-Chemistry) cut-off of 193.66, I couldn’t make it to the Government Medical College (GMC) of my town. Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Would the movie "Poove Unakkaga" be the super-hit that it was if Vijay had agreed to marry the heroine in the climax?
Answer: I really doubt! The movie remains a cult-classic because of its sad climax, rightly so. Poove Unakkaga is often considered to be the turning point in Vijay’s career. This movie would mark the beginning of many of his hits/ blockbusters. Not only that, it is also one of my favourite movies of vintage Vijay! With an endearing screenplay, decent enough comedy track, and a beautiful music album (who doesn’t like Anandham Anandham Paadum?!), it was quite the wholesome package for a mid 90s’ Tamil movie! Having said that, the entire movie is about how the hero would go to any extent to make sure the love of his life would unite with her lover against all odds! He does everything in his capacity and beyond to help the couple, only because of his true love for the girl. (Quite evident from the line from Anandham Anandham Paadum, ‘Un vaazhvil selvangal ellam ondraaga sernthida vendum; poovae un punnagai endrum sandhosham thandhida vendum’!) If his character were to move on, he would never have impersonated as the family’s grandson in the first place! The climax probably is the best scene of the movie. As a 90s’ kid, I know those dialogues by heart! Vijay’s disappointment, agony and helplessness are beautifully captured, especially when he goes “Andha ponnu lucky dhan ga; naa dhan unlucky! illana na love pannadhe andha ponnuku theriyama irukuma?!” (She’s a indeed a lucky girl! It is I, who am unlucky, for she doesn’t even know I was in love with her!). 27 years after its release, we still speak of the movie and this climax scene in the fag end of 2023, only because he chose not to move on! Had he married the Sangita character who never knew what she wanted and was okay with any decision taken by her family, chances are that Poove Unakkaga would have flopped and be long-forgotten by now! Whilst the climax, or probably the story itself, might be deplorable/ cringeworthy today, it’s totally understandable why it was a crowd-puller back in 1996! Come on, didn’t we have ′96 as late as 2018? (Picture taken from Google Images)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If you could pick any city to live in for a year, where would it be, and what would you do there?
Answer: Might be an unpopular answer, but ya… It is Delhi for me! I have been to Delhi only twice: once for an interview at St. Stephen’s College in 2014 and more recently for a scheduled PG counselling at AIIMS, New Delhi in 2022 (though I couldn’t actually attend it). Despite the multitude of problems plaguing Delhi, like air pollution for instance, I somehow love the city; I do not know why! I just enjoy the feeling of being in Delhi, traveling to Delhi or even transiting through Delhi. Maybe because it’s the National Capital and the realization that it’s the powerhouse of the country we all live in? Or because of the wide, clean and green roads of South Delhi and the associated posh vibes? Or is it all the beautiful girls out there?! I don’t know! Given a chance to pick up any city to live in for a year, it would definitely be Delhi! I would choose Delhi any day over Mumbai or Kolkata (though I have visited neither of those cities!). What would I do there? Nobody knows what’s in store for the future. My moving to Bengaluru transpired within a week; when I look back, it feels like a dream even today! Maybe Delhi might be in store too! Fingers crossed!🤞🏼

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What made your day today?
Answer: There are often long and hard days at work. Today was one such day! I write this answer lying down on my bed at the end of a tiring day, after ~60 km of up-and-down travel to workplace. I am currently posted at a Rural Primary Health Centre (PHC) in Bengaluru North. Today being Routine Immunization day, parents kept coming without a break to get their infants/ children vaccinated. Pregnant women also made it to the beeline to get their Td shot. There was hardly any time even for a short tea-break; from vaccinating the incessantly crying kids to making sure the ‘first-come-first-serve’ system is being followed to dealing with the recently introduced, time-consuming and buggy ‘U-WIN’ online vaccination portal greatly delaying the vaccination process, it was chaotic! To make matters worse, today we were short of two house surgeons (interns) who could’ve otherwise helped us with the process. Also, it was the first day for the only intern who was in attendance. I had to train him on the working (style) of the PHC, which included revision of basic treatment guidelines, drug dose calculation etc. In between all this, there was a surprise visit by one of our professors (from the parent institution I’m doing my residency) to the PHC to ensure attendance of all the PGs and interns posted. She was in conversation with the Medical Officer (‘the immediate boss’ of any PHC) and as a matter of courtesy, I went and greeted her. That is when the Medical Officer reflexly commented, “Bala is everybody’s sweetheart. Everybody loves him for his work and sincerity. He’s amongst the best PGs we get here. Not only that, the way he communicates things to people and speaks is just awesome. Nanagenadru magaLu iddidre ivnge kottu maduve maaDstidde! (Kannada for ‘If only I had a daughter, I would get her married to him’!)” My professor replied, “That’s true, he has all the traits of a good community physician!” Though I did feel shy and wondered if I’m worthy of that much praise, it felt so good to be acknowledged for my work, that too in the middle of such a hectic day at the hospital. This small, yet hearty conversation about me between my professor and senior physician made my day!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: When was the last time you did something for the first time?
Answer: Today! For the first time in life, I took a bike taxi. It’s been almost a year since I had given my car for servicing. Also, given that I will be driving down to my hometown (300+ km away from Bengaluru) this Wednesday, it was high time I did it today! After dropping off my car at the service showroom, to get back home, I booked a ride through Rapido and chose the ‘Bike’ option. The wait time was around 5 minutes. I was apprehensive about only one thing: if the ‘captain’ (as cutely referred to by the app) would provide me with a helmet. I was not aware of the policy because it was my first time using the app itself, leave alone bike taxi. The captain arrived on time. Much to my relief, he gave me a helmet that he carries routinely for the pillion riders; the ride began once I told the OTP. It was an enjoyable ride, thanks to the cold breezy evening at Bengaluru! I reached home after what was like a 15-minute-journey. I have always wanted to go on a bike taxi, as the idea of riding pillion on a bike with a stranger seemed fancy. Though I had never been on a bike taxi earlier, this was not the first time I had seen/ heard of it. Bike taxis are quite popular in East Africa, where they popularly go by the name ‘boda-boda’; I have personally seen people use them in their daily walks of life in Tanzania and Rwanda, during my visits to these countries. On a parallel note, there has been a bitter relationship between bike taxi drivers and autorickshaw drivers in India, especially Bengaluru! There are multiple videos making rounds all over social media, where autorickshaw drivers accuse bike taxi drivers of spoiling their livelihood. With the Government of Karnataka’s recent move of making bus transport free for ladies, this hatred has only aggravated. Today, I was able to witness it through my own eyes. The drop-off point I had chosen had an autorickshaw stand right next to it. The bike taxi captain stopped about 100 metres before the auto stand and said, ‘Sir, alli autodavaru nintirthaare; problem aagbiduthe! Nimmanna ille drop madtini, bejaar madkobedi!’ (Sir, autodrivers will be there near the drop location; it’ll become a problem! I’ll drop you here itself, kindly do not get me wrong!). I duly got down and thanked him for the smooth ride. Wondering whom to feel sorry for: the autodrivers who have lost business, or the poor unemployed youth trying to make a living as bike taxi drivers, I walked forward!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Why doesn't the Karnataka government rename Rajajinagar and Kamaraj Road to Kannada names?
Answer: For the simple reason that both were national leaders/ political figures, and not merely politicians limited to Tamil Nadu. C Rajagopalachari aka Rajaji was the first and last Governor General of independent India. He was also the Union Minister for Home Affairs between 1950 and 1951.[1] K Kamaraj was the president of Indian National Congress (the only major political party at that time) between 1964 and 1967. Not just that, he is known as the ‘kingmaker’ of the then Indian politics for he was responsible for making Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi the Prime Ministers after the demise of Jawaharlal Nehru.[2] Both Rajaji and K Kamaraj, therefore, have a nationwide appeal and historical importance. Also, let’s not forget that both of them were active players in the Indian freedom struggle! With Bengaluru being the capital of the Indian state of Karnataka, at least I don’t see a compelling reason to rename the said area and the said road! Bro, but what about the kannadathana of the city? Well, The above list is only a handful, based on my knowledge of the areas in and around my home in Bengaluru. There are hundreds of other areas/ roads/ places in the city named after Kannadigas, or depicting Kannada culture. For instance, Sampige Road at Malleshwara is named in Kannada after the flower that’s widely available and sold in the area. Having said all that, a couple of Tamils’ names doesn’t have to warrant a riot! (A frame from Rajajinagar; from my phone’s gallery)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Have you ever had a kid behind you on an airplane kicking the seat the entire flight?
Answer: Not a kid, but a lady! More than a decade back, I was on an Emirates flight from Lagos to Dubai. It was an overnight flight, with dinner service almost a couple of hours after take-off. I reclined my seat sometime after the seatbelt sign was switched off. ONE FIERCE KICK! I turned back only to realise that it was not a kid, but a middle aged lady; and that it was not by mistake, but deliberate! (Looking at the stare she gave me). I immediately reverted the seat to its original position, deciding to deal with this matter after dinner. Dinner service got over; lights were dimmed. Since it was an overnight flight and at least 5 hours of journey were left, I wanted to sleep. I slowly reclined my seat, once again! No sooner did the lady kick again, with double the previous force :/ This time I lost my cool; I simply called the flight attendant and explained the situation. After a stern warning from her, the lady behind did not repeat her act! But I’m sure she would have cursed me deep down. What I do not understand is how such people have double standards: she wanted her own seat reclined, and also the front row passenger’s NOT! Why not travel business class, madam?! Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What personal bad news would you like to share today?
Answer: Well, not exactly bad; but an unpleasant, anachronistic news! I tested positive for COVID-19 today. I was alright until 4 days back, after which I started feeling uneasy even though there were no outward symptoms. Later, I developed typical URTI symptoms like sneezing and blocked nose. Soon, I also developed fever which was on & off, controlled on taking anti-pyretics. Two days back, I also had a bad sore throat which forced me to get an RT-PCR test done for COVID-19. Lately, many patients with similar complaints had been coming to the Primary Health Centre I currently work at. The overall number of COVID-19 cases is also on the rise in Bengaluru recently. Despite taking adequate precautions, somehow I seem to have caught the infection :/ COVID-19 is a nostalgic disease, indeed! I spent most of my MBBS internship days treating COVID patients. The disease was then dreaded by everyone, with terms like quarantine, lockdown, isolation, mask, ICU, oxygen etc. doing the rounds everywhere and everyday. Today, after multiple ‘waves’, the disease has become too commonplace like common cold. Yet it’s very much benign unlike before, thanks to the universal adult vaccination drive in India. Fun fact is that I never caught this infection in 2020 while treating the sickest of patients on ventilators who were counting their days, but now in late 2022 when COVID has become an almost forgotten entity! Importance of masking up and maintaining physical distancing? You don’t say!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Is it necessary to clean shave in medical college?
Answer: Not necessarily. Whilst most medical colleges do have a dress code, there’s no written rule that boys will have to clean shave. However, many professors (Females >>> Males) believe that a ‘clean shaven face’ is an integral part of professionalism, and frown on beards. They enforce it during their lectures, practical classes and clinical postings. Most of us, especially during the early years of MBBS, religiously follow their instructions. With passing time, adherence to the same decreases :D One of our microbiology professors was fond of picking on boys with the slightest growth of beard (Moustache was allowed as most Tamilians are not comfortable shaving off their moustache). I had only then (2016) developed a liking for the French beard and tried to sport one. He promptly called me to his desk and the conversation went as follows: Sir: Why have you not shaved your beard? And…what is this style? Me: Sir, I… just… Sir: Are you sporting this beard because you like it, or because… someone special asked you to? Me: Sir, sir… nothing like that! Sir: Because, if that’s the case, I won’t ask you to clean shave! Otherwise, you’ll have to. Me: I’ll shave off, sir :P But, I never shaved! After second year MBBS, nobody really asked us to trim/ shave unless the overall appearance was rugged with unironed clothes/ unkempt hair etc. We just had to maintain a decent dress code, especially while attending the clinical postings. In fact, one of the surgeons openly said having beard was OK, provided we maintained it properly. He himself tried and sported different beard styles regularly! An interesting scenario: Final practical exams! A popular saying in the medico community of India goes like ‘MBBS degree is not taken, it is given!’. One never knows which (external) examiner has what opinions about looks. Few of them still have opinions like ‘First impression is the best impression’, ‘Face is the index of the mind’ etc. and judge the student based on whether they have shaved/ not; wear clean, ironed aprons/ not; wear polished shoes/ not and what not! Few of them are much more open-minded and evaluate the student(s) only for their clinical competence. Naturally, medical students leave no stone unturned to pass these final exams! Because it is difficult to predict which of the above two categories the examiner would belong to, none of us took a chance during our final practical examinations. It is that season of the year, where you would spot clean shaved faces everywhere in the campus! Even the ‘big macho tough guy’ would look like a child :D (Me on the day of last practical exam of first year MBBS!)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If I take an MD in physiology after an MBBS, is it successful in a small town?
Answer: Does the small town have a medical college? Is that a government medical college? Is there a vacancy for Assistant Professor of Physiology post, that you can apply for?! If the answers to the above questions are a yes, then ‘Yes, you will be successful!’ Nevertheless, your MD (Physiology) degree will place you at a higher pedestal than any MBBS doctor. Moreover, unlike, say MD Microbiology (which is essentially everything about all microbes), physiology is very closely linked with the clinical specialities as it deals with the functioning of human body, after all! Any doctor with a sound knowledge of physiology will be a successful person at that. Like General Practice? The combination of the knowledge of functioning of human body and *the MD degree* will do the magic! With dedicated and committed patient care, minimal investment and word-of-mouth marketing by happy patients, your private practice will flourish. Most of the times, this earning exceeds that of a junior level faculty member in a government medical college. You’ll just need patience! Changed your mind to move to a city? The number of medical colleges is increasing every passing year; prospects of your earning a decently paying teaching job isn’t that difficult! My hometown Pondicherry alone has a whopping 8 medical colleges for a population of around 2.5 lakhs! Also, how about starting a YouTube channel, writing an MCQ book or joining a PG coaching platform as mentor/ faculty part time?! Best wishes!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Have you ever faced a language barrier in your college?
Answer: No! I was fortunate enough to get into a government medical college of my home state. Almost 100% patients coming to our hospital speak Tamil, the local language. It’s mainly because the population here itself is linguistically homogenous. Contrary to what few people think, nobody speaks French in Pondicherry :D Most people coming from other states (North India included) and settling/ intending to settle down here, also eventually learn to speak Tamil. So I did not face any language barrier during the course of 5.5 years of my MBBS. In college, I got friends & batchmates from Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Delhi, Haryana, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar etc. We converse(d) in English for all practical purposes, though they used to talk in Hindi amongst themselves. I can recall only two instances in the whole of my college life, where I had to face a language barrier in my own city. In all probability, I would be moving out for my Post-Graduation in a few months. Hope I overcome the language barrier I may have to face!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Can Indians and Pakistanis be friends?
Answer: If somebody’s nationality is the sole criterion that stops you from making or being friends with them, then it would never qualify as friendship in the first place; you would also need to introspect your thought process in that case! At the same time, I do not opine all friendships are meant to stay. We have all had best friends who became strangers later. Was it because the friend was a different national? Well, not really! Whether two people can be friends depends on a lot more factors than just nationality, in fact nationality should never be a factor that makes or breaks a friendship. I have friends from every country that I got a chance to visit. If this question comes from a religious context, the answer is of course ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ Few friendships also have the privilege of transforming into love stories that culminate into marriages! Do we have such Indian-Pakistani love stories? Hell, yeah! If this question is from a political context, the answer is still ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ If the question is from a linguistic context, the answer is still ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ I guess the whole ‘India vs. Pakistan’ idea is a very local one restricted only to these two countries. Once I am out of India, or a Pakistani friend is out of Pakistan in a foreign land, we’re both recognised as Asians! In Africa, I’ve been asked if I’m a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or an Indian, looking at my skin tone. They don’t even know unless we tell them; we’re just Asians to them. Pakistan, or India, doesn’t matter to them as long as they get business. Similarly, Indians and Pakistanis share workplaces, businesses and friendships in several parts of the world, especially in the Gulf and the UK. When such smooth dealings are possible outside our native lands, why not here? While I was on a street tour in Dubai, the cab driver was kind enough to go out of his way and show me every possible place that could be covered within half a day. He would have definitely figured out that I was from India; he was still friendly, he was still doing his job with utmost dedication! Guess what? He was a Pakistani! And there’s this Pakistani gentleman whom every medical student on Earth admires and reveres. He’s a role model to thousands of budding doctors and is undoubtedly one of the greatest medical teachers the world has ever seen - Dr. Najeeb! Do you think any sane Indian would not want to be friends with him, just because he’s a Pakistani?!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is something you're not proud of but you continue to do?
Answer: Being a night owl! It is 1.30 AM now, as I write this answer. I’m not one bit proud of staying awake late in the night. I know it is all the same technically, either reading late in the night or rising early and utilising the whole day. But the problem with being a night person is, I am finding it very difficult to get up before 9 AM. This is the time my mother leaves to work. I say bye to her, lock the main door, and again sleep till 10 o’ clock. Thus the start of the day itself feels very lazy. By the time I shower and finish my breakfast it is easily 11 o’ clock, which is quite a late start to a day, right?! Hardly two hours and it is lunch time. I do not postpone my lunch break beyond 1.30 pm due to personal reasons. This short interval of just 2.5 hours between two major meals of the day isn’t very healthy, medically speaking. There are other reasons not to be proud of being a night owl. I miss out on the early morning sunrise, Suprabhata/ Vishnu Sahasranama, potential walk/ jog on the beach road and of course having the breakfast as soon as it’s made! I’m also not being that idealistic guy from an idealistic family having shower early in the morning! Overall, I feel I lose a lot of productive time. These days, it has become a vicious cycle: I get up late, consequently I’m not drained of my energy even after 10 PM, I stay awake (mostly preparing for my PG entrance exams) usually till 2.30 AM or sometimes 3 AM and the cycle continues. One advantage though is, I never get the kind of a silence I get at night during the daytime. There are absolutely no distracting voices or noises - a perfect environment to read/ revise/ focus on anything I am at. That said, I am still not convinced with this whole night owl scene, and yearn to be an early bird with a proper sleep cycle. I tried changing my sleep pattern a couple of times, but failed! I hope I do so before it’s too late.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is the most badass thing your parent has ever done?
Answer: Early 2000s… Maybe 2003 or 2004. Back then, I do not think high speed broadband Internet connections existed, at least at our hometown Pondicherry. We had this age old BSNL dial-up Internet connection, connected to the landline telephone. It required us to log in with a password every time we needed to access the internet. Also, while using internet, if one was to pick up a call on the landline, internet connection would get disconnected and the log-in procedure had to be repeated. We had an internet connection at home mainly because dad had to check E-mails when not at work and clear them off before the next day. Needless to say, it was not an era of smartphones. The very concept of internet was fascinating for my sister and me! We felt thrilled being able to get information about anything with just few clicks, browse different websites and communicate through E-mails with family contacts living as far as in the USA. Contrary to Google, Yahoo’s home page itself would be awesome with multiple featured news items, links directing to Mail, Answers, Messenger, Stock market, Weather and what not! I guess it still is like that, although the traffic on the site is multifold less than Google. But what caught our eyes every time was ‘GAMES’! Yahoo used to have this concept of ‘Downloadable Games’. Only the trial version of these games could be downloaded. Full version required us to pay online in US Dollars, which was unimaginable for us. The trial version included 60 minutes of free game play, after the expiry of which only 5 minutes of gameplay would be allowed every time the game was opened. We were permitted to download only one such game every week or every 10 days, as the internet bills were also relatively expensive those days. We were allowed to access the internet only when our father was at home. We didn’t have a choice either, because only he knew the password. This was mainly to prevent us from downloading multiple games and escalating the internet bills, and of course the keep a check of our activity in the internet. Our dad was and is still a workaholic. Even when he was at home, he used to be occupied with office work. We had to ask him to log-in for us whenever we had to download games from the internet or every time the internet connection got disconnected because mom picked up a random landline call🙆🏻‍♂️. This was very frustrating for us, as kids! We promised him we would not exceed the download limit and not use the computer when he was not home, and requested for the password. He did not budge. The password was a mystery known only to him for few more years, until one day we both sneaked in close to him and saw him typing it! My sister and I never felt more fooled or dumber till date in our lives! The password was no complex alpha-numerical word or phrase, but ‘studioworks’, after all! Studioworks was the name of that particular model of LG monitor, boldly printed over it, right in front of our eyes! *Facepalm🙆🏻‍♂️🙈* This, by far, is the most badass thing my parent(dad) has ever done! Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: How do I overcome superstitions?
Answer: In an Indian context, most of what we now recognise as superstitions had a scientific basis/ reasoning. Over the days, people forgot the same and started blindly following these practices which is why they became ‘superstitions’. But that’s not the case always! One example that I readily recall is the ‘shunning of cutting nails in the evening (after sunset)’. This practice was originally in place because there was no electricity even as early as a century back. Our ancestors did not want any of these dirty cut nails to accidentally get into the dinner plates. Back in those days, lanterns that used oil weren’t as bright as today’s LEDs and CFLs. At the same time, few so called ‘superstitions’ are based on science or at least scientific theories! For instance, there is this rule in most of our homes not entertaining anybody to sleep with head facing the North direction. This is backed by so many articles[1] and studies dealing with areas like magnetism. So the ideal solution is to question the superstition! Identify if there were any plausible grounds in the past for the very establishment of the superstition like in the ‘nail-and-the-sunset’ story and its relevance today. If the answer is yes and the logic doesn’t hold good now, do not follow it! If the answer is no or you’re in doubt, and following the said superstition doesn’t affect your life, keep following it! You never know for what reason it is being followed, it might be scientific or might not be! But hey, there’s nothing to lose. Coming to the same examples, this is what I do! I have no hesitation in cutting my nails after sunset or evening because we have perfectly well lit housing these days, and the nails go straight into the bin. Also, who cuts nails near the dining area? So, one superstition disappeared. Talking about the sleeping direction, my head faces the East when I sleep. Why be a rebel and take pains to sleep with my head facing the North, to just disprove a strong belief, that I am not 100% sure is false?! When in doubt, go to Science :)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What shocked you today?
Answer: Post completion of my MBBS, I’ve been preparing for my MD entrance exams. Two exams got over recently. As I will not be able to get a branch of my choice based on these exams’ scores, I’m appearing for the INICET exam to be held on 14th November, 2021 and preparing for the same. I had given a mock entrance exam couple of days ago and was reviewing the answers this morning. So, today was basically like any other day… until I saw this! One of my professors, who also happens to be a Kannadiga, had posted this status on WhatsApp. I could not process it. I was blank. I replied to her, asking what happened, why a black and white picture with broken hearts?? She was quick to reply that he had suffered a ‘massive heart attack’ and passed away! Praying this to be a rumour (there are way too many death rumours of late), I immediately googled ‘Puneeth Rajkumar’. There were many news articles that showed he was ‘critical’ and being treated in the ICU of a popular corporate hospital in Bangalore. A YouTube search also yielded similar results, with rather scary portraits. I rushed to the living room, switched on the TV and saw all Kannada news channels covering this single news: Puneeth Rajkumar’s critical health condition. I was still hopeful because not one news channel reported he had passed away! (Puneeth Rajkumar receiving treatment in ICU) (Chief Minister (of Karnataka) in conversation with the Rajkumar family) Once again, I asked my professor what actually was happening. She told he was no more but it was not yet official. To support her claim, she also sent a forwarded audio wherein a doctor from the hospital where Puneeth sir was admitted tells he had passed away, inspite of all their resuscitative efforts. She also sent a forwarded picture where Puneeth sir’s lifeless covered body was lying in the hospital stretcher. (These became public moments later) I was beginning to feel numb and emotionally troubled furthermore. I called up one of my friends in Bangalore. As we were talking over the developments, the TV screen flashed the much dreaded, most unfortunate news, I or anyone who follows Sandalwood, could’ve imagined. (Actor Puneeth Rajkumar no more) Like any other Kannadiga or Sandalwood fan, I was dumbstruck. This news felt like it came out of nowhere. Not in our wildest dreams would any of us have imagined such an untimely death for Sandalwood’s power star. As time passed by, more and more information kept pouring. As if the news of his very death was not enough, there were more and more heart wrenching information like he was perfectly alright this morning; he had been to gym; he had tweeted wishing his elder brother’s latest movie success; he had danced on a stage during the promotional event of the same movie, just two days back; he had been an active part of a music director’s birthday celebration last night; he was the chief guest of a hospital’s inaugural ceremony three days back; and what not?! (Puneeth sir’s tweet dated 29th October at 7.33 AM!! Life is freaking unpredictable!) Hundreds of celebrities tweeting condolences, sharing stories on Instagram, WhatsApp statuses filled with Puneeth’s photos… One thing was universal and common about all these posts. All that people could say was, ‘I cannot believe this happened/ can’t process this/ this is not possible’ and the like. Because that’s how it was and still is! It’s almost 12 hours since the bad news was out and millions of us are still SHOCKED. (One of the thousands of tweets, from Telugu actor Mahesh Babu) Puneeth sir was known for his fitness, after all! When such a fit and healthy person himself succumbs to heart attack, it only raises serious questions on our own lifestyle and its potential dangers. This is a bit clichéd, but I’m not able to stop myself from thinking of this - even Puneeth sir himself would’nt have anticipated something like this, a death like this! He’s one person in the industry with zero controversies. As is commonly pointed out, nepotism is there in South Indian film industry too. But unlike other regions, nobody becomes successful in Southern cinema just because their father/ family was successful in the industry! Puneeth was not a product of nepotism; his current fanbase was hard earned, thanks to his acting, dancing abilities, non-conformation to pointless punch dialogues… the list goes on. He had carved an image for himself in Sandalwood. Interestingly, whilst all the above facts about his professional life are true, nobody who was asked to speak about Puneeth, following his death, talks of his career! All that they could reminisce and share about him is his unassuming personality, ever-friendly nature, his philanthropy, his smile🥲, his impeccable professional conduct and his pure soul. Isn’t that what success and life’s victory ultimately is? (He (Puneeth Kumar) sponsored the education of students from more than 45 schools) *Just one of his many philanthropic activities* On a personal front, I’ve myself watched only one of his movies, Raajakumara (2017) which has the famous song Bombe Helutaithe. This movie became the highest grossing Kannada movie ever at that point, beating Mungaru MaLe (2006). But I’ve heard/ watched most of his songs; eagerly waited for and watched his Kannadada Kotyadhipathi, the Kannada adaptation of Kaun Banega Crorepati?; seen his interviews on YouTube and ardently followed him on social media. Most importantly, I do not know how to feel about this! On Wednesday (27th October, 2021), I felt like singing Neenade na, which is a super-hit song from Puneeth sir’s recent Yuvarathnaa movie, sung by Armaan Malik and Shreya Ghoshal. Usually I just hum/ sing and let it go. I don’t know what had gotten on me the other day, I also recorded as I sang! It could’ve been some other song (I love old Kannada classics too), from some other movie! But no, it was a Puneeth song! This makes me feel devastated even more. I feel a strange unexplainable connect, now. I have collected few photos from the internet, attached them to the aforementioned audio clip, made a video and uploaded it on YouTube. Whilst I’m not a trained singer, I consider this surprisingly coincidental recording as my humblest of tributes to the person who’s loved by ~6 crore Kannadigas (yes, he had no haters) and lakhs of other Indians! So this is what shocked me today! I was in shock, still in shock…(probably in the ‘stage of denial’ of grief, as explained by American psychiatrist Elizabeth Kübler!) Mathe hutti banni, Puneeth sir!❤️💔 Signing off by dedicating two lines from his own song Bombe Helutaite from the movie Raajakumara! Ninnanu padedha naavu puneetha! BaaLu nagu nagutha!! We are the lucky ones to have (have had)you! Live happily always!! (in your afterlife😇)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If Tamil Nadu is exempted from NEET, can the whole of India ask for an exemption from the NEET?
Answer: I am not sure of the legal probabilities with respect to this question. But the method of admitting students into MBBS has to be a state decision. If admission through Board Exam score is what they want, give them that! I cleared my higher secondary exams in March 2014. I am from Pondicherry and we follow(ed) the Tamil Nadu State Board syllabus. I can vouch for it. It was of high standard and exhaustive. Recent TN textbooks are even more exhaustive and wholesome, preparing the student for NEET-PG exams. Question: Then why is it opposed? Why should the students of TN/ PY not give NEET-PG? Answer: Why should they give?! I was admitted into the Government Medical College of my state based on my board exam marks. What mishap happened? I can safely tell I’m doing fine. I can reasonably approach and confidently treat all illnesses and diseases an MBBS graduate is expected to treat; I can give public health education at village and community level; I can provide basic wound care that includes suturing and dressing; etc. On the contrary, clearing a so-called competitive exam and entering a medical college gives no assurance that the student would automatically become one of the best doctors of the country. It is the dedication and commitment one has during the course of his or her MBBS which decides the kind of professional they become in future. Moreover, hundreds of my seniors from Pondicherry and Tamil Nadu, who were admitted into MBBS based on Higher Secondary Board Exam marks, are in very prestigious institutions like AIIMS-New Delhi, PGI-Chandigarh, NIMHANS-Bengaluru, etc. doing their residency now. Where comes quality of medical professionals here? There are thousands of successful, contemporary doctors from TN and PY who got into MBBS (until 2016) using their board exam marks. Chennai is still one of the leading cities in the world for Medical tourism! So, what is in an entrance exam?! After all, admission through board exam marks was also by a carefully designed counselling system. ‘Biology-Physics-Chemistry (BPC) cut-offs’ used to be as high as 199.9 for General Category students and many a time not less than 197, even for reserved categories! Scoring that high in board exams is not a child’s play! Only the best of the best hard workers could achieve that feat. Now why introduce another tough exam for entry into MBBS? Isn’t it like an insult to their year-long hardwork and efforts to fare well in the Higher Secondary exam? If board exam marks don’t guarantee qualified doctors in the future and only an exam like NEET can do the job, then why have schools and board exams?! Those kids who intend to become doctors should be able to straightaway enrol themselves in coaching classes, right?! But that’s not the system in place! The only instance where I advocate entrance exam for admission to MBBS is for filling up of the All India Quota (AIQ) seats in state medical colleges. Each state follows a different syllabus. It would be illogical to come up with a ranklist of students with different state syllabi for MBBS admission into the AIQ seats available in the medical colleges throughout India. (Do NOT immediately suggest unification of syllabus throughout India! Anything that has zero diversity is detrimental for a country as big as India!) Therefore, each state should ideally have its own MBBS admission strategy for the 85% state quota seats. This may be through the Higher Secondary Board exam marks or through a common entrance test for the state candidates alone. This decision has to be based on the interest of the majority; in this case - concerned students, teachers and parents. In addition, candidates of all states must have the option to sit for the All India level common entrance exam (AIPMT/ NEET) which would be the single entrance exam for filling up of the 15% AIQ seats across Indian medical colleges. வாழு, வாழ விடு! (Live and let live!)

Question: Why are most Hindus vegetarian?
Answer: I’m a Hindu. I’m a vegetarian. But, am I a vegetarian because I’m a Hindu? I guess not! I was probably inducted into vegetarianism as a child because I was a born into a Hindu family. But I remain a vegetarian simply because I like to be one. There have been instances where my friends wanted me to take non-vegetarian food. Personally, I can’t tolerate the smell emanating from omelettes or that ‘eggy’ staunch from cakes. Also, as multiple other answers clearly explain, not all Hindus are vegetarians. On the contrary, we have heard of vegetarians and vegans of other major religions, as well! To conclude, I feel, at present times there’s little relevance between food habits and religion/ caste. One may be born into a vegetarian family, but he/ she remains a vegetarian because of his preferences, his education, his surroundings, his contacts etc. It all boils down to being vegetarians by choice! Question: What is the saddest moment you have seen in a movie or TV?
Answer: Background story: A father (widower) of four kids. He is bankrupt as he has recently been suspended from his job on charges of embezzlement. His only family members are: -Elder Son, who has despised his family and lives in the United States, so much so that he wouldn’t even come back to his mother’s funeral. -Younger son, who is a prodigal with no proper educational qualification and constantly at loggerheads with his family. -Elder daughter, married off to a typical, rich patriarchal Indian family, which is not supportive of her going to a job or visiting her dad or giving him money. -Younger daughter, who had a Poliomyelitis attack as a child and is physically challenged. -An extremely orthodox brother-in-law who deals with his own financial and family problems! This gentleman has turned to alcoholism for his solace, further worsening his poverty. At this juncture, he plans to get rid of his only burden, his younger daughter, by marrying her off to a prospective groom. But as fate would have it, nobody comes forward to marry the girl as she is physically challenged. Even otherwise, many reject her, as she is not from a well-to-do family! Finally a guy approaches her dad, asking her hand in marriage. Apparently, he’s not behind money or looks or anything, but he wants to marry her for who she is! Sounds wonderful, doesn’t it? But, the story isn’t that simple or merry! When the father brings up this proposal to his daughter, she comes to know that the prospective groom is 46 years old! He emotionally blackmails her that it was her mother’s last wish to get the girl married. He argues that her mother’s soul wouldn’t rest in peace, in case she refuses to marry the only guy who came forward to marry her. Having no choice as a helpless daughter to a drunk widower, the poor girl agrees to meet the boy. At this point, the dad is taken aback. He was expecting some retaliation from his daughter. But the fact that she instantly agreed to his proposal makes him feel guilty. In order to overcome it, he tells her, ‘It’s not a compulsion. I’m not telling that you must marry him. Just see him tomorrow; if you like him, well and good! Otherwise, all that we have to lose is a cup of coffee!’ The distraught daughter replies, ‘Don’t worry dad, I don’t think a 46-year-old(or young?!) groom would probably need sugar to his coffee!’ This is by far the saddest, and probably, the deepest scene I have ever seen on television! It captures the vulnerability of not just physically challenged, but also most poor girls in India. From the 1990s Kannada television series, Mayamruga aired on DD Chandana and later on Zee Kannada. Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What has been your experience with probiotics? Has it helped you?
Answer: December 2017 It was winter vacation after my second professional MBBS exams. I was at Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, with my dad. (Morogoro; PC: Google) I still don’t know if it was the ‘not-so-good’ food taken in that restaurant or me acquiring some endemic infection (Traveler’s diarrhoea) from the exotic Morogoro, I developed severe fever. Soon, loose stools followed. I was rushed to a local hospital at Dar es Salaam, where they ruled out Malaria by a rapid test (Malaria is endemic there, and they proceed any further only after ruling it out). Then, I was diagnosed as a case of ‘Bacterial infection’ and started on Intravenous fluids (drips), intravenous antibiotic - Ceftriaxone (for 3 days) and generous doses of Paracetamol. Guess what? My fever subsided, my diarrhoea worsened like never before. I could not move out of the restroom and was having close to 20 episodes of loose stools per day! I was severely dehydrated and too weak to even walk. That’s when I contacted my professor over WhatsApp. She told me it was ‘Antibiotic induced diarrhoea’, something I could not decipher at that time. Antibiotics, when taken over a long time or in increased doses, tend to affect the balance between good and bad bacteria. In the event of eliminating the harmful bacteria, the beneficial ones are wiped out as well, leading to intractable diarrhoea. The treatment was simple. She asked me to stop the antibiotic (already stopped) and take probiotic supplements. Probiotics are essentially these ‘beneficial bacteria’ that are important for the Gastro-intestinal system to maintain a decent functioning environment. These probiotics usually come in sachets as powders. They are meant to be mixed with water and drunk as a solution. (Probiotic sachets, from my phone gallery) I took these probiotics for 2 to 3 days, along with lots of water and fruit juices. Diarrhoea disappeared gradually. I regained strength and was able to do all my daily activities. But by this time, it was already time to fly back to India! (From my phone gallery)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What made you happy today?
Answer: Making a correct diagnosis! Yesterday, one of my relatives had called me. She complained of ‘feeling too cold even in normal room temperature, when others around don’t feel so’. This is what is known as ‘cold intolerance’ in medical terms. At the same time, it could also be ‘chills’, which is a symptom of conditions like Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) or Malaria. But most of the times, it is associated with fever. In this case though, there was neither fever nor any UTI complaints (increased frequency, burning sensation during urination or lower abdominal pain). So I landed up with a provisional diagnosis of hypothyroidism, of which cold tolerance is a classical symptom. Moreover, hypothyroidism is several times more common in ladies than men. Hence I asked her to get a Thyroid Function Test (TFT) done. The test results came out today. As expected, her TSH level was above normal limits! This is a finding consistent with hypothyroidism. Not surprisingly, her T3 and T4 levels were normal, indicating her to be a case of what we call ‘subclinical hypothyroidism’. Well, that’s what made me happy today - being able to pick symptoms and make a provisional clinical diagnosis even before a lab test would confirm the same. Of course, this is not an out-of-the-world, rare case that needs extra intelligence to pick up. But as a freshly graduated doctor, making such correct diagnoses gives me immense happiness and motivation to keep going. Happy doctors’ day to all fellow doctors!🌸

Question: What is the nearest river to your place?

Another name found in literature is Varahanadhi (Varaha river), though there is another river of the same name in Southern Tamil Nadu. After flowing a relatively shorter course than most other popular rivers in South India, Sankaraparani enters the UT of Pondicherry in a village called Manalipet. Sankaraparani receives various tributaries throughout its course, the details of which I’ll spare. Being an easterly flowing river, it finally drains into the Bay of Bengal as ‘Chunnambar’, after receiving its final tributary - the Guduvaiyar. Though there are many historic temples along the course of this river both in TN and PY, the most popular tourist spot is the Chunnambar boat house. It is among the ‘must see’ places of almost all tourists who flock to Pondicherry. It’s always crowded with tourists that I’ve not been there even once, despite being a local :P (Chunnambar boat house; PC: Google Images) A boat from here takes one to the ‘Paradise beach’ which is a narrow stretch of land in the Bay of Bengal coast. Question: What is the most unforgettable experience you had while grocery shopping?
Answer: I wouldn’t say unforgettable, but it is definitely a fond memory! August 2016 I had just come back to Pondicherry, my hometown, after a month’s vacation at dad’s in Tanzania. My mom hadn’t returned. Back home, my grandmother wanted me to take her for grocery shopping to refill supplies at home. She had asked me to pick whichever powdered drink I wanted. Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Can computers create smells?
Answer: Ah! This question reminds me of an instance from my school days. I was in the tail end of eleventh standard. Board exams were going on for either SSLC or Higher Secondary (12th standard) appearing students. Our school also being one of the centres for these exams, naturally gave half a day’s leave (in the forenoon, when those exams happened) for all other classes. Our classes would begin by 1.30 or 2 PM and go on till 6 PM. Consequently, we all had a nice time on those days, having the liberty to get up late and to chill till afternoon! My routine at that time was pretty much spending time on ‘Yahoo! Answers’, which was a thing then, reading random articles on Wikipedia and playing online/ downloaded games on our computer. April 1, 2013 (if my memory is not bad) It was one such day. As usual, I opened Google Chrome (which was and still is my default browser) and the home page ‘Google’ opened. The otherwise plain Google page had something extra and strange. It read ‘Google Nose BETA’! Mind you, I was not aware of the date at all nor did that link feel funny/ unbelievable. So… I clicked it! The following page opened. As a (dumb) child, I had always wondered, ‘If photos, audios, videos, vibrations (like in Play Station 3) which involve our special senses can be transferred, why not smell and taste via technology?! After all Science advances every day!’ Now, for such a person, this ‘Google Nose BETA’ seemed very convincing! I thought, ‘Finally, another breakthrough in science; Google have proven themselves yet again!’ (Yes, as kids born in the 90s, stuff like Google Images and Google maps which were introduced in the 2000s seemed so ‘cool’ to us, given that we started off with Encyclopaedias and state road map booklets). Moreover, it was BETA afterall, meaning Google were just trying to establish a new technology which was in its baby stage. There were various odour options available for one to smell/ sniff. All one needed to do was to click on the interested frangrance and sniff the monitor as Google’s new technology emanated it from your monitor! I think I chose ‘Lemon’ as it is a nice fragrance to begin with! And hey, Google played its April Fools’ day prank successfully on me! The only relief is that I was not alone, but there were millions of others across the globe unsuccessfully trying to sniff their monitors in hope of getting to devour their favourite scent. Below are what others tried! What I came to know later was, Google was infamous for such April Fools’ day pranks even before 2013 and continued them till 2019![1] And it was me who had been ignorant till then, inspite of being a daily internet user. ‘Google’s April fool day Joke’ was not featured in 2020 as the world was amid COVID crisis. For the record, I don’t think any computer or smart gadget can ‘create’ smell, at least till now!

Question: Is eye, cns, bone not taught completely in pathology in 2nd year of MBBS? Our college is just teaching important topics. Do I need to read all or just these topics?
Answer: Yes, these topics were not completely taught in our college too! Pathology is a very broad specialization. At second year MBBS level, we are just introduced the various concepts in pathology an undergraduate doctor would require for his understanding of the common diseases. This, essentially is, what general pathology is about. In systemic pathology, most diseases that are commonly encountered or relevant because of their dreaded prognoses are dealt with. Mind you, this itself takes 1.5 years! When I open my Robbins today, there are not only heavily highlighted pages, but also untouched brand new pages! That’s how it is. Few topics are purposefully ignored as they will be covered in great depths (including pathological aspects) in other subjects! Best example is ‘Infectious diseases’, for which a separate subject, Microbiology is taught in second year. So is the case with However, certain aspects of these topics are not dealt with so much detail as in Pathology, even in dedicated subjects. Also, what you learn in these chapters in Pathology can be glaringly different from what you will learn in future. For example, when you hear the word ‘Retinoblastoma’, this is what would (should :P) come to your mind! When it is asked in pathology exams, only this aspect will be tested upon! But once you’re done with third year MBBS, it would always be remembered as Anyway, to answer your question, it is more than enough to read whatever is taught in these topics :) Also, remember that these are of high yield for your university exams as questions come invariably from these small topics! A tumour from CNS (menigioma/ Schwannoma/ astrocytoma), CSF findings in different types of meningitis, osteomyelitis (just for the mention of ‘sequestrum’, ‘involucrum’ :D), one of the skin malignancies (SCC/ BCC/ melanoma) are all favourite topics of most pathologists and some sure-shot questions!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is your salary? Are you happy with it?
Answer: I’m a doctor and I’m paid ₹5,000 per month. Obviously, I’m not happy with it. I’m currently a Compulsory Rotatory Residential Intern (CRRI) doctor/ House Surgeon at the Government Medical College - Hospital of Pondicherry. We started our internship on February 19th, 2020. A month later, COVID-19 was in the news and soon our hospital became the state’s COVID designated hospital and all other services were shut. Today, with 13500+ total cases and 211 deaths, Pondicherry tops the country in the number of positive COVID-19 cases per million! Ever since there were interns in our hospital (from 2015), this amount of ₹5000 has been the standard monthly stipend. No payslip, no Government Order, no whatsoever. It comes to ₹161/ day which is far less than most daily wage labourers in the country. Even worse, the stipend is not credited to our bank accounts every month. It is usually credited at the end of three months as ₹15,000. This stipend amount is the least of all Government Medical Colleges in the country. Funny fact is that ours is allegedly the country’s most expensive Government Medical College, tuition-fee wise. It used to be ₹70,000/year when I was a UG student. Now, I understand it is 1 lakh+ per year, from my juniors. Multiple attempts in representing this issue to the government, including indefinite student strikes, RTI complaints etc. yielded nothing. Whilst this stipend amount is not acceptable even during normal times, imagine working day and night during a pandemic period for ₹161/ day. Our valuable training period is also lost in the name of COVID-19. We have completely lost hope on the government regarding stipend hike. Therefore, we have not resorted to any more strikes. We have been posted in all areas of the COVID hospital including COVID wards, COVID ICU and casualty. While this unhappy and unrewarded feeling will definitely continue to prevail, I’m sure this has, not in anyway, affected the healthcare we provide to our patients, nor will it in the future. This holds good, COVID or not :) (Picture from my phone gallery)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is everyone doing during the coronavirus?
Answer: As such, my routine remains undisturbed. Coronavirus has probably made me more cautious and self-protective at workplace. I have been working as an intern/ House surgeon at the Government Hospital of my town. I have completed two postings viz Ophthalmology and Otolaryngology. Currently, I’m posted in the department of Dermatology. Over the last few weeks, I have keenly been following the news and the rate at which Coronavirus is on the rise. From 28 cases 15 days ago, to 165+ cases and 5 deaths today, the magnitude of the disease is scary. We have always followed universal precautions at workplace like frequent hand washing, using hand rubs after attending to every patient and wearing masks where required. I would say, the emphasis and the frequency of these activities have increased. From sweepers to the Heads of Departments, everybody is seen adorning masks; hand sanitizers are used like never before; anybody who coughs attracts extensive attention from by-standers; so on and so forth. We have strictly limited the number of outpatients that come to the hospital and very stringent rules have been laid out as to who and how many can accompany the patients. No elective surgeries are being done and non-COVID19 inpatients are being discharged. Adequate medications are being given and all patients are asked to review in NOT less than 4 weeks. On a personal note, I’ve started to avoid any type of social gathering. No hangouts with friends, not even that long walk in the beach. All of that can wait! I go to work because I have to. Had I not been a doctor, I would have happily remained home doing things I love. The service of doctors, be it for screening Corona suspects or tracking contacts or treating the affected at the earliest, is indispensable. Most other professionals can work from home. Remember, hospitals are melting pots of all kinds of infections and Corona is no exception given the current scenario. I kindly request people to refrain from going to hospitals for minor illnesses like body aches or refractive errors. It can only get you and your loved ones COVID-19. So, here I am, working at my hospital at the time of a major crisis.

Provided the time constraint, I could even miss my flight in this process. For the above said reasons, I’ve stopped carrying check-in luggage altogether. Question: What was the oddest question you were ever asked by airport security?
Answer: May, 2011 Back then, my dad was working for a Container Glass Industry in Nigeria. We (Mom and I) had gone to visit him during the summer break. Almost a month later, it was time for us to return home. Place: Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, Nigeria. There were two Emirates flights to Dubai (our connecting airport en route Chennai) per day, one that departed in the afternoon, reaching Dubai in the night. The other one, departing at around 09:30 pm and reaching Dubai early morning next day. We were booked in the latter. Now, this route (Lagos - Dubai) is a very busy and fully-booked one, considering the worldwide air connections available from Dubai and also the trade in Nigeria. This reflected on our flight too. There were very long queues for boarding! Felt like it would take ages for economy class passengers to be called. (Emirates has an ‘all wide-body’ aircraft fleet and hence boarding is always a Himalayan task). The scene was exactly like below So, we were waiting, worn out and apathetic. Suddenly, an announcement was made: “Passengers travelling with infants and kids are now invited to board the aircraft”. OK! So when this happened, I was 14 years old, a 10th grader at school! I wasn’t an infant (obviously ;) ) NOR A ‘KID’! Therefore, neither mom nor I reacted to the announcement. Cutting the crowd, a lady from the security came, straight towards us! And she directly talks to my mom (with a strong African accent), “Madam, why are you standing here? We just called passengers travelling with kids!” I retaliated reflexly, “I’M NOT A KID”. She was too cool to get offended. She asked a simple question and gave an all new definition to the term ‘kid’! “Are you married?!” So, that was the oddest question that I was ever asked in an airport, considering the fact that I was a 14-year old adolescent male! LOL. P.S: I replied “No”, and she confirmed my ‘kid’ status and made us board with other ‘kid’ families! (Pictures taken from Google images)

Tech Computer Science & Engineering (CSE) at Pondicherry Engineering College (PEC). One or two months into college, I was well settled with the course and never looked back nor repented for not getting into Medicine. First year went well and I happened to be the topper of my batch in the 2nd semester exams. We were on summer vacation after which second year classes would begin. Meanwhile, 12th standard board exam results (of the next batch) were announced and that’s when all the confusion began! Surprisingly, this time the BPC cut-offs were very less (exams that year were a bit difficult); my dad applied my marks for MBBS admission once again! And my state merit rank shot up an unbelievable 100 ranks from Rank 150 of the previous year to Rank 51, paving way for my admission to the Govt. Medical College I dreamt of joining a year ago! After so much dilemma whether ‘To quit or not to quit’ engineering, I finally took the decision to quit Engineering, and joined MBBS It was tough. I was a ‘fresher’ once again! I had moved from a place where I was one among the best, to a new college to pursue my then long-forgotten dream of doing Medicine. There were hundred other fresh, enthusiastic, curious minds just imported from school! Now, things were serious. As is widely known, MBBS is no fun; first year is considered to be one of the toughest phases in the five-and-a-half year course. Cramming Anatomy, remembering the endless molecules and metabolic cycles of Biochemistry, and understanding the complex Human Physiology required endless nights of studying. Plus college hours were always longer relatively in first year. But the worst part is there is no ‘arrears system’ for the first years in MBBS! This means, at the end of one whole year of such tedious days and tiresome preparation, if one fails in the final exam(s) due to some unforeseen reason, he/ she would not be allowed to attend second year classes; and most importantly, these students would be grouped as something called the ‘additional batch’. To fall into the additional batch was horror to any first year medical student because this meant they would never reunite with their original batch and remain separated for the rest of the course (5 years!) as a small batch! They have separate classes and a totally different schedule, from clinical postings to university examinations - everything! Sadly, they are also looked down upon by most, if not all. Given this scenario, it sent me chills down the spine to even think of failing my first year exams. I was already a year late in joining medical college after school; my school friends, who were elsewhere, were in their third year of college already! And in the event of me not clearing my first year MBBS exams, I would be a big failure in life (or so I thought :D), imposing it myself on me because it was I who chose this! So, I organised my study holidays well, spent ample time with my books and made the best out of my capabilities. I gave the exams with full confidence and waited for the results. After a month or so, one fine evening, the much dreaded results were declared. Circumstantially, there was nobody home at the very moment! I did not have the courage to open the results web page. As said earlier, that result meant a lot to me and would greatly affect my future prospects and education! Heartbeat soared, my hands had begun to tremble by then. Finally, I entered my register number and the following page flashed in front of my eyes! I could just see those three green coloured ‘pass’ to the right side! I closed the website at once and…. broke down into tears, happy tears!! Like never before! I called up my parents (who were in Tanzania) and conveyed the rather happy news in such a tearful voice. It took me almost half an hour to compose myself and reopen that page. Only then did I realize my marks were pretty good. I had scored a distinction in all the three subjects, indeed! That was one of the most overwhelming moments of my life and probably the happiest too!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Is it better to teach GI system by going through each section of the alimentary canal, or by clustering different parts based on common functions?
Answer: The conventional teaching has always been Anatomy wise. I still remember my pathology classes where the GI pathology was taught starting from Oral cavity (Leukoplakia, erythroplakia) and ended with Colo-rectal Carcinoma. Now, in General Surgery classes too, it has always been region wise. Like we had a series of 4 to 5 classes each for Stomach, Pancreas, Hepatobiliary System etc. till date. This way, a student would better correlate the anatomy, physiology and biochemistry of the concerned organs and appreciate the pathology better and also understand the principles of medical and surgical management. That said, it is the reverse when it comes to clinical teaching that happens in wards/ Outpatient set-up. One should always discuss a disease symptom wise rather than region wise. E.g.) A complaint of ‘vomiting’ can be due to myriad causes. Questions like ‘Receptors involved in vomiting, Non- GI causes of vomiting, significance of colour and odour, and drug induced vomiting’ are good examples as to how the student would get an overall idea about the condition and link different subjects/ domains involved. This would bring in lot of discussion, differential diagnoses and greatly improve critical thinking. This would train the upcoming doctor to treat the patients better, with more confidence and rationale.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Is it true that doing yoga can cure type 2 diabetes? I was watching Chasing Life with Dr. Sanjay Gupta: India. An Indian said that his HA1c fell from 200 to 110 and does not use medication anymore.
Answer: When it comes to Diabetes, prevention is the only choice. There is no known ‘cure’ for Diabetes or most diseases for that matter. E.g.) Hypertension (unless it is secondary to some tumor such as pheochromocytoma or other curable conditions), Hypothyroidism etc. Also, a person with HbA1C of 110 is not compatible with life! You’re probably talking about the Fasting Blood Sugar (FBS) levels.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: How many Dravidian languages other than Kannada have native words (not those borrowed from Sanskrit) which starts with the letter 'ha'?
Answer: Thanks for A2A Goutham R (ಗೌತಮ್ ಆರ್) As a Tamil speaker, I can say there is no word in Tamil that starts with ‘ha’. The Tamil Alphabet has 247 letters and it doesn’t include ‘ha’. In fact, the letter ‘ஹ’ was developed/ introduced just for transliteration purposes. So when there is no such letter, there can be no words either! Also, the above said use is often condemned and words beginning with ‘ha’ are often Tamilized! —Mostly in cases of proper nouns (Names). E.g.) Hindu - இந்து (Indu), Haran - அரன் (Aran), Hosur - ஓசூர் (Osur) Moreover, Tamil has its own equivalents to all the Sanskrit words and the influence of Sanskrit even sans ‘ha’ is very less.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is most important in learning English?
Answer: I feel mastering the grammar is more important than any other aspect in learning English, or any other language for that matter. Pronunciation of many words varies widely from region to region; there is no single accepted or rather ‘correct’ pronunciation. However, standard pronunciation can be developed by watching international news channels, listening to online radio stations or watching English movies (does not really serve the purpose, considering the usage of slang words and colloquialism) Vocabulary, on the other hand, is quite challenging. Building one’s vocabulary is a lifetime process. So, it can be taken slowly. Learning a certain number of new words (say, five) and constructing sentences using those words would really help a novice. Even otherwise, good company like native speakers or co-learners will prove to be of great help in improving and improvising the vocabulary. Therefore, I feel, Grammar is the most important. Because, building a strong vocabulary and developing ‘perfect pronunciation’, still with grammatical mistakes, is a big turn-off! A person with poor grammar is always looked down upon, at least in a professional set-up!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If you are much more interested in the pathogenesis and diagnosis of medical conditions than treatment and patient care, does it make you a bad doctor?
Answer: Not at all! I can see myself in this question. I'm a person who loves the pathogenesis (the mechanisms through which a disease evolves) more, than actually knowing about the various treatment options available and cramming them up. (I'm a UG medical student still, nearing Finals). For the same reason, I enjoy reading Robbins more than Harrison. We have been students of Science since years and continue to be; even before we were students of Medicine, we were students of Science! That said, Science can explain anything on Earth and where it fails to, progress has to be made. As far as Medicine is concerned, from the most common symptoms like fever to complex complications, all major diseases (causing significant morbidity and mortality) have scientific basis as to what happens at the cellular (sometimes, even molecular!) level. I feel, in the pursuit of learning to 'just treat' more and more cases and clear off the long queues in OPDs (for which we are trained, at least as UGs), one shouldn't forget the fact that, it is still the Biology that guides all this treatment and its efficacy. Failure to give importance to pathogenesis of diseases, and underestimating the role of research in molecular biology, are what have led to the various lacunae that we have today in treating advanced and rare diseases. End of the day, it's all team work. Surgeries (at least major ones) don't happen without pathologists' or radio-diagnosists' reports or opinion. Microbiologists, whose role is often undermined in recent times, 'diagnose' (of course in lab) deadly infections and issue the most needed 'Drug sensitivity reports', which act like a life-safer many a time, considering the highly resistant bacterial strains and increasing ICU admissions. They are people who love 'diagnosing' more than treatment; they are doctors after all! And the role of Biochemistry in 'diagnosing' Medical conditions is indispensable, without which there is no 'treatment'! The simplest example, I can think of in this regard is the 'treatment' of Diabetes Mellitus. Knowing that blood glucose is increased in Diabetes Mellitus through biochemical tests, and the knowledge through evidence that Insulin reduces the level of blood glucose is what led to the use of various forms of Insulin in therapeutics today! We have come a long way from bovine insulin to recombinant DNA insulin. Thanks to researchers who work on pathogenesis and diagnostics! Going one step ahead, studying for years together the molecular mechanisms of Glucose metabolism and the various receptors involved, today we have an array of drugs known as 'Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs' which have come out to be the saviours of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients. And the increase in life expectancy of these patients, before and after Metformin, I needn't comment I believe! Ultimately it is like 'Any doctor can treat a disease, but only a doctor passionate about the science (pathogenesis) behind, and knows what to look for in different reports (diagnosis), and of course, appreciate with understanding, the signs and symptoms, treats the patient!'. Also, only such doctors are the hope of the future. (We still have deadly diseases that have no treatment or vaccines). This is my humble opinion. Regards, Balakrishnan R.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is your favourite word in your native language?
Answer: I was born and (being) brought up in Pondicherry, India. So my native language is Tamil. There are a lot of favourite words that I can think of, Tamil being very ancient and one of the most beautiful langauges. But, I would like to share that one word which awed me at the very first sight! It is 'நோயீனிகடத்தி' (noyeenikadathi) which means 'vector' (Biology) A 'vector' is an agent, usually an insect, that carries a disease-causing-organism in it. It goes about spreading infectious diseases. The above Tamil equivalent, of course, is not an ancient word. But it has been aptly coined as medical science evolved. It conveys the very definition of a biological vector! [நோய் (noi) = disease, நோயீனி (noyeeni) = Pathogen/ disease causing agent, கடத்தி (kadathi) = transmitter] I first came across this word when we went on a visit to The 'Vector Control Research Centre' (VCRC), as a part of our field training when we were posted in the Department of Preventive and Social Medicine (PSM) a.k.a Community Medicine. Not only was I impressed by the commendable, high level research and training activites going on in this institute, but also I thoroughly enjoyed learning this new word which has now become my most favourite Tamil word!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Do you speak Telugu?
Answer: I don't really speak Telugu at the moment (except for a few broken sentences), but I'm trying my best in learning the language so that I can speak fluently. That said, I do listen to people speaking Telugu and can make out the typical 'urban' coversation mixed with English words. I have quite a few Telugu friends: some - natives of Andhra Pradesh/ Telangana/ Yanam (one of the four enclaves of the Union Territory of Pondicherry) and few Telugus who have settled for good here in Pondicherry (my native place). They are my main source of learning Telugu. Them being the kind people they are, patiently teach me the essential basics, correct my sentences, grammar and pronunciation. Secondly, I get to watch Telugu movies in theatre (Telugu movies have a reasonable demand in Pondicherry since there is a sizeable Telugu speaking population based in Pondicherry itself and also students from the above said places), the most recent ones I watched being Rangasthalam and Geetha Govindam. Talking about the reading and writing part, I would say I'm better at reading and to some extent writing Telugu than speaking, thanks to my Kannada lineage. I can read, write (which have helped me in reading Telugu - explained later) and fluently speak Kannada. Kannada and Telugu scripts are close to each other (very few letters and the accents are different) and if somebody knows one, mastering the other doesn't take more than week or month if rigorously attempted. This is my humble try at writing Telugu ( I meant to write 'My name is Balakrishnan. I live in Pondicherry. Hope you are fine.' Blame Google translate if the translation is funny or wrong :P :D) Last, but not the least, Telugu songs are close to my heart. Be it the Carnatic music kritis/ varnas (I play the violin and these were my first lessons!) or contemporary Telugu music, they are there on my playlists! A long drive is never complete without listening to atleast a couple of Telugu songs. In fact there are certain remade / dubbed (from Tamil) Telugu movies whose songs I'm more confident with the lyrics and also singing (credit to repeat mode on mobile phone and promotion of these albums in the social media) than the original Tamil versions! Best examples I would cite include songs from the movies 'Kaala' (no offense Tamilians…but 'Chittemma' , I feel, is way better than 'Kannamma'), 'Ye Maaya Chesave' etc. So folks, that's the story of me and Telugu. Looking forward to learn more. Hopefully my next answer about Telugu would have few Telugu sentences!!

Question: Is the Kasaragodu part of Karnataka?
